Once Revolutionary, this 20-Year-Old American Yacht Is Now Asking for $20M
28 photos
Photo: Denison Yachting
Is it really worth spending nearly $20 million on a yacht below 50 meters that’s been around for two decades? Beyond what industry experts have to say, the answer is highly subjective. No matter what, the 2006 Christensen that made an appearance at this year’s Fort Lauderdale International Boat Show hides a trailblazing origin making it much more exciting that what can be seen superficially.
When someone today is looking at a decades-old yacht, it’s hard for them to imagine and to feel the enthusiasm and sheer excitement of what that yacht represented 20 years ago, when it was officially presented to the world. Today, Crili might seem like just another yacht below 50 meters from Christensen, but the truth is that Crili was a true pioneer at the time of its launch.
To be able to fully appreciate what this American yacht means today, we must take a short trip down memory lane and try to picture it as the fresh Christensen delivery that everyone in the industry was talking about in 2006. Launched as Hull 028, Barchetta was the newest in an already successful series of tri-deck 157-footers (48 meters). It was similar to its predecessors, but also very different.
Exactly twenty years ago, in November 2006, Mike Smith was writing in Power &Motoryacht about the powerful debut of the intriguing new Christensen. The shipyard’s strategy as the time was to deliver three yachts per year, which meant they were starting to build a new boat in the 157-foot series every three months.
Photo: Denison Yachting It was the magic of semi-custom yachts – perfect for the busy owners who wanted the freedom to personalize their luxury boats, but without the waiting time associated with a custom yacht. Most of the work on Barchetta was done in-house, except for the interior design, officially handled by Jacqueline Mann Design, but with major input from the owner who, according to Dudley Dawson, who reviewed this yacht in the Yachting Magazine a year later, in 2027, was “a lady”.
While building on the earlier successful deliveries in that same series, Barchetta took on a trailblazing role that would make it unique. First, it became the first-ever Christensen yacht to sport a bulbous bow, specifically for improved fuel efficiency and better range. To achieve this, Christensen worked with the prestigious New York-based Webb Institute, and planned to apply this innovation to all future yachts in the series.
Boasting a massive maximum displacement of 800,000 lbs, Barchetta was also the heaviest Christensen at the time (explained, according to Mike Smith, by the use of 0.75-inch stone slab for all the interior). Yet, what made it remarkable was the proven 17-knot top speed, even at this weight. This performance was apparently also possible thanks to the innovative bulbous bow.
Beyond the engineering upgrades, Barchetta flaunted what everyone at the time agreed was a spectacular Art Deco interior. Maximalist, bold, and openly flamboyant, the owner-curated original interior design featured dramatic elements like black resin inlays inspired by the Chrysler Building, custom glass artwork in the owner’s en-suite, and striking decorative accents in hot red (including the leather upholstery and bed linens).
Photo: Denison Yachting This pure shade of red became a signature symbol for the yacht, beyond the purely decorative accents – from the nameplate that looked stunning against the classic white hull backdrop to the engines themselves, a pair of large MTUs. Another statement feature was the original owner’s personal art collection of expensive crystal and glass pieces, including Lalique.
In fact, as Dudley Dawson vividly describes, it looked as if Barchetta’s interior design in neutral tones and contrasting black inlays was meant to become the perfect canvas for the owner’s Art Deco collection. This is even more unusual considering that the 2006 Christensen was intended for charter operations from the start.
Apparently, the owner made sure to set up specific security measures for all the artwork throughout, as well as protecting it against any kind of damage, and even the precious upholstery was specifically treated to be water-resistant, for the same reason.
As it inevitably happens, the 2006 yacht that was the largest Christensen at the time and the first one to sport a bulbous bow, changed ownership several times, and its original sparkle faded more with each new change of hands.
Photo: Denison Yachting Reportedly, Crili’s most recent owner was a Florida-based billionaire, the late Alfonso Fanjul, one of the two billionaire brothers associated with a sugar empire. Forbes called them “The Florida Sugar Barons” with Cuban roots and an important presence in Florida. Alfonso Fanjul passed away earlier this year, and perhaps that explains why Crili joined the market and attended FLIBS just a few months later.
This year, when it was featured at FLIBS twenty years after its launch, the renamed Crili was no longer one of the most impressive and innovative American yachts around.
Still, it’s just as coveted as brand-new yacht in the same size category, mainly thanks to the continuous upkeep and recent upgrades. A full paint job, the rebuild of its main engines and transmissions, plus a professional engine room repaint are some of the highlights completed in 2023, 2025, and 2026.
In 2025, Crili has also completed its mandatory 20-year class survey, a confirmation of its ABS classification that allows it, among other things, to activate as a charter yacht. Considering all the upgrades completed over the years, plus the yacht’s original Christensen DNA and proven charter history, the $19.7 million price tag seems justified, even for a yacht this age and below the unofficial superyacht size threshold.
Photo: Denison Yachting Boasting interior volume just under 500 GT, Crili can easily accommodate at least 14 guests, and even more. The classic configuration features a full-beam, main-deck owner’s suite, and five more guest suites. Since the beginning, dedicated quarters for a generous ten-person crew were also more spacious and better equipped than the standard at the time.
Beautiful amenities onboard include an elegant formal dinner reminiscent of the yacht’s original Art Deco aesthetic, a fully-equipped gym, a light-filled main salon showcasing the original glossy wood paneling throughout, and a large jacuzzi, plus grill facilities, on the sun deck.
As soon it had dived into charter operations, Crili packed a hefty toybox, even an exciting mini submarine for three. Today, jet skis, inflatable water toys, and larger tenders are available for charter guests. Just as important, Crili has the fuel storage capacity to support extended cruising without too many stops. A perfect vacation yacht in every way, Crili combines the comfort of a floating mansion with the proven track record of charter success.
Although, unfortunately, few people today remember what this beautiful 2006 Christensen meant at the time and how dazzling it was in its original era, Crili remains one of the most important yachts in the American shipyard’s history, and an excellent US-built pleasure craft overall.
Photo: Denison Yachting The American shipyard that started building composite luxury yachts in Vancouver, Washington, in the late 1990s, delivered yachts that are still famous today, such as John Staluppi’s Casino Royale and Tiger Woods’ Privacy. Crili didn’t make headlines like some of these better-known Christensens, but it’s just as remarkable, and won’t most likely need to wait too long for its next owner, even with that intimidating $19.7 million price tag.
